title: A Holy People, Chosen Because God Loved Them
summary: Moses commands Israel to destroy the seven nations of Canaan, to make no treaties or marriages with them, and to tear down their altars and idols. He grounds the command in Israel's identity as a people holy to God, chosen not because they were many or great but because God loved them and kept his oath. He promises blessing for faithfulness, tells them not to fear stronger nations, and warns that the idols' silver and gold must not be kept.
story: Chapter 6 set love for the one God at the center of Israel's life and warned that prosperity in the land could lead them to forget him. Chapter 7 turns to the other threat: the gods of the peoples already living there. If Israel will be tempted to follow “the gods of the peoples around you” (6:14), then how are they to live among those peoples? Moses' answer is severe and uncompromising, and the chapter holds that severity next to one of the tenderest statements in the Old Testament about why God chose Israel at all. The rest of the Bible will show how poorly Israel kept this chapter, as Joshua and Judges report Canaanites remaining in the land and Israel adopting their gods.
historical:
The chapter's list of seven nations (verse 1) is a traditional roll of the peoples of Canaan, and several of the names are hard to pin down. Canaanites and Amorites are well attested in ancient texts as broad names for the region's inhabitants. The Hittites named here are probably groups living in Canaan rather than the Anatolian empire of that name, though the relation between them is debated. The Jebusites held Jerusalem until David took it. The Girgashites, Perizzites, and Hivites are known mainly from the Bible. Seven is also a number of completeness in Scripture, and the list stands for the whole population of the land.

The religious objects named in verse 5 are well documented. Sacred pillars were standing stones set up at shrines. Asherah was a goddess, known from texts at Ugarit on the Syrian coast as the consort of the high god El, and the Asherah poles were wooden cult symbols associated with her. Inscriptions found at Kuntillet Ajrud in the Sinai, from around 800 BC, speak of Yahweh and his asherah, which suggests that some Israelites later did exactly what this chapter forbids and joined Israel's God to Canaanite worship. For the debate about the book's date, see the note on Deuteronomy 5.
cultural:
Marriage in the ancient world was never only a private matter. It bound families together, and it usually brought the gods of each household into the new home. The ban on intermarriage in verses 3 and 4 is given a religious reason, not an ethnic one: “they will turn your sons away from following Me to serve other gods.” The Old Testament itself shows that the concern was faith rather than blood, since Rahab the Canaanite and Ruth the Moabite are both welcomed into Israel. Ruth becomes David's great-grandmother (Ruth 4:17), and Matthew's genealogy later places Rahab in David's line as well (Matthew 1:5). Solomon's foreign wives, by contrast, are blamed for turning his heart to their gods (1 Kings 11).

The word Moses uses for Israel as God's “prized possession” (verse 6) comes from the world of property and kingship. A related word in Akkadian, the language of Babylon and Assyria, is used for a king's private treasure, set apart from the general wealth of the realm. Israel is God's personal treasure out of all the peoples he owns. The “hornet” of verse 20 has been read literally, as a figure for panic sent by God, or as an image of some foreign power that weakened Canaan before Israel arrived; the text does not explain it.
literary: The chapter moves in three waves, each ending with a reason. Verses 1 to 5 give the command about the nations, and verse 6 gives the reason: Israel is holy and chosen. Verses 7 to 16 explain that choice and the blessings that come with faithfulness, closing with the command renewed. Verses 17 to 26 answer an imagined objection, “These nations are greater than we are,” with a call to remember Egypt, and end with a warning about the idols' silver and gold. Key words recur deliberately: love (verses 8, 9, 13), keep (verses 8, 9, 11, 12), and the language of devotion to destruction, which returns in the last verse, now aimed at Israel itself.

outline.t: No treaties, no marriages, no altars left standing
Chosen by love, not by size
The blessings of keeping the covenant
Do not fear the greater nations
The idols' silver and gold must be destroyed

doctrines.note: God keeps “His covenant of loving devotion for a thousand generations” (verse 9). His faithfulness is the fixed point; Israel's blessing depends on responding to it. The covenant began with God's oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and God's choice of Israel flows from that promise.

Israel is “a people holy to the LORD your God” (verse 6), set apart for him. Holiness here is first a status God gives and then a way of life that follows from it, which is why the people must refuse the worship of the nations around them.

The chapter refuses every explanation for Israel's election except God's love. They were not chosen for their numbers or greatness; they were the fewest of all peoples. The logic is almost circular on purpose: God loved them because he loved them. Grace has no cause outside God.

Even the precious metal on an idol is a snare (verse 25). Israel is not to keep what is attractive about false worship while rejecting the rest. The final verse warns that anyone who takes a devoted thing home becomes devoted to destruction with it.

words.note: Segullah, treasured possession. The word is used of a king's personal treasure (1 Chronicles 29:3 uses it of David's own gold and silver). Applied to Israel (verse 6, and Exodus 19:5), it says that the whole earth belongs to God, but Israel is his in a special, cherished way. The New Testament applies the same idea to the church.

Bachar, to choose. It is the Old Testament's central word for election. Here God's choice of Israel is explicitly not based on anything in Israel: not their numbers, their strength, or, as chapter 9 will add, their righteousness. The word is used in Deuteronomy both of God choosing a people and of God choosing a place for his name.

Chesed, steadfast love, loyal kindness, or, in the BSB, loving devotion. It is love that keeps its promises, the loyalty of one who is bound to another by covenant and goes beyond what is strictly owed. It is one of the great words of the Old Testament for God's character.

Cherem, a thing devoted to destruction. Something under cherem belonged to God so wholly that it could not be used by people. In verse 26 the word turns on Israel: whoever brings a devoted object home becomes cherem too, as Achan later does in Joshua 7. The ban was not a mark of ethnic favoritism.

christ: The New Testament takes the language of this chapter and gives it to the church. Peter calls those who belong to Christ a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and a people for God's own possession (1 Peter 2:9), drawing on Exodus 19 and passages like this one. Paul says Christ gave himself to purify for himself a people for his own possession (Titus 2:14). The chapter's insistence that God chose Israel only because he loved them runs straight into the New Testament's teaching on grace: God shows his love in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8). At the same time the church's holiness is no longer expressed by war on its neighbors. Christians are sent into the nations to make disciples, not out of them to destroy, and the separation the New Testament asks for is from idolatry and sin, not from people.

hard.q: Did God command Israel to wipe out whole peoples, and was it ever carried out?
hard.a:
Verse 2 commands Israel to “devote them to complete destruction,” and verse 16 says, “Do not look on them with pity.” Read plainly, this is a command to destroy the population of Canaan, and it is one of the most troubling passages in Scripture. Several things in the chapter itself complicate a simple reading. The same passage forbids intermarriage and treaties with these nations (verses 2 and 3), which would be pointless if no one were expected to remain. Verse 22 says the nations will be driven out little by little. And the reason given is consistently religious: the danger is the altars and gods, not the people's ethnicity, and the ban applies equally to Israelites who take what is devoted (verse 26).

Interpreters weigh these facts differently. Some take the command as literal but unique, a judgment on Canaan's sins limited to that time and place, never to be repeated. Others read the language of total destruction as standard ancient war rhetoric, meaning decisive defeat, and point out that Joshua and Judges describe many Canaanites still in the land. Others see it as a stage in revelation, God working within the moral world of the ancient Near East while moving toward the fuller light of Christ. Readers who hold Scripture in the same high regard differ here, and none of these answers removes all the pain. Christians of every view agree that the New Testament gives no warrant for violence in God's name.

questions: God chose Israel not because they were impressive but because he loved them. How does it change you to know that God's love for you does not rest on your size, success, or goodness?
Moses warns against keeping the silver and gold from idols even while rejecting the idols themselves. Where are you tempted to keep something attractive from a way of life you know is wrong?
The people feared that the nations were greater than they were, and Moses told them to remember what God had done. What fear in your life needs to be answered by memory?
